Brent fell about 5% to near $93, and Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi (Axios, NPR). Fremont is foggy, with a high of 71.

stories.title: Massie re-files Hegseth impeachment, forcing a House vote by Wednesday
stories.summary: A privileged resolution with eight articles must get a floor vote within two legislative days, and Democrats plus a few Republicans could carry it.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, re-introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, Nov. 9 (Fox News, Washington Examiner, ABC News). Because the resolution is privileged, House leaders must act on it within two legislative days, which puts the vote on Wednesday at the latest. Leaders can try to table it or refer it to committee, which would likely kill it. Most of the articles concern the Iran war, and others cite strikes on alleged drug boats, Yemen and the capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro (Washington Examiner, Fox News).

Massie first filed in September, but GOP leaders cancelled votes and sent members home early, pushing the fight past the midterms. Republicans then lost heavily on Nov. 3, and Fox News and Axios report that several House Republicans privately believe the measure could pass. Axios notes that defeated members have little left to lose, and Fox says absences among Republicans who lost their seats could tip the count. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" that he is a "hard yes." He said the Democratic caucus would "have that conversation" Tuesday morning.

Hegseth called the effort a "sham" led by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman," and Trump has said he has "every intention to keep him" (NBC News, Washington Examiner). House Oversight Chairman James Comer declined to defend Hegseth and said there are "a lot of questions" (Washington Examiner). Rep. Warren Davidson called the push an effort to scapegoat Hegseth (Fox News). Even if the House impeaches him, removal needs a two-thirds Senate vote, and CNN notes conviction is unlikely.

CNN's analysis adds that impeaching Hegseth could let Democrats avoid the riskier fight over impeaching Trump himself. Leaders of both parties have reasons to dislike the vote, which is why the procedural fight over tabling matters as much as the final tally.
facts: Massie's measure has eight articles, most tied to the Iran war.
As a privileged resolution it needs a House vote within two legislative days, by Wednesday.
Jeffries called himself a "hard yes" on ABC's "This Week" on Nov. 8.
Trump says he intends to keep Hegseth, and Comer says there are "a lot of questions."
Senate removal would take two-thirds, and CNN calls conviction unlikely.
stories.left: Democrats argue that a defense secretary who steered the country into a costly war of choice without clear congressional approval has abused his power, and that the War Powers Resolution means something only if Congress enforces it. Jeffries says Hegseth undermined national security and that the war drove prices up for ordinary families. They note the push comes from a Republican, which makes it harder to dismiss as partisan. Voters just delivered a verdict on the war, and Congress should act on it before the lame duck ends.
stories.right: Conservative critics argue that impeachment is for high crimes, not for disagreement over a war that the commander in chief ordered and that Hegseth carried out. They see a lame-duck stunt by a defeated congressman, plus a way for Democrats to relitigate the war instead of funding and finishing it. Some on the right share Massie's worry about unauthorized strikes, but say the remedy is war powers votes and the defense budget, not removing the Pentagon's civilian chief during active talks with Iran. Davidson calls it scapegoating for election losses with many causes.
stories.next: Watch the Democratic caucus meeting Tuesday morning and a possible motion to table by Wednesday.

stories.title: Lame-duck Congress faces a Dec. 11 funding deadline, the defense bill and a nominee rush
stories.summary: Lawmakers returned with five weeks to avoid a shutdown, and a short-term extension looks most likely.
story: Congress returned to Washington this week for a crowded lame-duck session, with government funding set to run out on Dec. 11 (NPR, ABC News, Fox News). The stopgap that expires then passed the House 370-48 before the midterms. Reporting from NPR and others says leaders are most likely to pass another continuing resolution rather than 12 full-year bills, because lawmakers lack the time and the political will for a full process.

Iran war funding has emerged as a flash point, according to coverage of the session (NPR, ABC News). The House and Senate also have to pass the National Defense Authorization Act before the end of 2026. Senate Republicans want to confirm as many of Trump's remaining nominees as possible before they lose control of the chamber in January. Fox News described the stretch as a "brutal" one with leadership races in both parties on top of the legislative load.

The Hegseth impeachment vote adds to the pressure this week. Some appropriators have said Congress tends to end up with a large year-end package when it faces a lame-duck deadline, while others in the GOP want to avoid the Christmas omnibus tradition. NPR's read is that a kick-the-can extension would hand the harder choices to the new Congress.
facts: Government funding expires Dec. 11.
The expiring stopgap passed the House 370-48 before the midterms.
A new continuing resolution is the likeliest outcome (NPR).
The NDAA must pass before the end of 2026.
Senate Republicans want to confirm nominees before losing control in January.
stories.left: Democrats say a clean stopgap is the responsible choice, because they will hold the House in January and can set spending priorities then. They want Iran war money to face real scrutiny rather than ride on a must-pass bill, and they argue Republicans should not rush lifetime appointments through a chamber the voters just took from them.
stories.right: Republicans argue that the majority they still hold should be used to finish the job: confirm nominees, pass the defense bill and fund the government and troops without lapses. They say a short extension avoids a shutdown that would hurt military families during a war. Some want a full-year bill to deny Democrats a new fight in the spring.
stories.next: Watch for a continuing resolution text in early December and the NDAA vote before the Dec. 11 deadline.

stories.title: Democrats call for a national data center moratorium as Republicans split
stories.summary: Sanders and other top Democrats seized on 40 of 41 local ballot wins, while some Republicans back pauses of their own.
story: After voters sided against data centers in 40 of 41 local measures across 10 states on Nov. 3, Sen. Bernie Sanders posted "National data center moratorium now," and other top Democrats called to rein in the AI buildout (CNBC). The measures ranged from outright bans on new construction to pauses on planned facilities and limits on energy use. A Gallup survey from May found seven in 10 Americans oppose data centers near them.

The right is divided. A Fox News opinion piece argues that Sanders and the far left want to stall AI and data centers, which would give China an opening in the AI race. Yet some Republicans have joined the restrictions: Michigan's GOP Senate nominee backs a one-year moratorium, Pennsylvania's GOP nominee for governor supports a pause, and Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller called for a temporary halt on new hyperscale projects (Washington Examiner, CNBC). Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has pushed an AI bill of rights that protects local communities' right to block projects.

The Trump administration has downplayed the effect. Kevin Hassett said "the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren't affected by these ballot initiatives" (Axios, CNBC). Rep. Rob Bresnahan's Local Control Protection Act would limit companies' ability to sue towns that reject projects. Newly elected governors are not calling for permanent bans.
facts: Voters backed data center restrictions in 40 of 41 local measures in 10 states.
Sanders called for a national moratorium.
Some Republicans, including nominees in Michigan and Pennsylvania, back pauses.
Hassett says near-term projects are not affected.
Seven in 10 Americans opposed local data centers in a May Gallup survey.
stories.left: Democrats argue that communities are paying for AI buildouts with higher electricity bills, water use and noise while the gains go to a few companies, and that voters have said so at the ballot box. A pause lets regulators catch up on grid costs and safety before more capacity is locked in.
stories.right: Conservative critics argue that a moratorium would hand the AI lead to China, raise costs and kill jobs, and that local concerns are better met by siting rules and making developers pay for grid upgrades. Others on the right see community control as a conservative value and back local vetoes.
stories.next: Watch for moratorium bill text in the new Congress and for data center projects delayed in Texas and elsewhere.

stories.title: Bay Area transit tax passed; BART expects about $310 million a year from fiscal 2028
stories.summary: Regional Measure RTM averts deep BART and AC Transit cuts, but BART says a structural shortfall remains.
story: Voters approved Regional Measure RTM on Nov. 3, a sales tax meant to raise about $1 billion a year for Bay Area transit (San Francisco Chronicle, KQED). Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties pay 0.5%, and San Francisco pays 1%, over 14 years. Nearly 65% of Alameda County's share goes to BART operations. KQED's headline called it a "death spiral averted."

The alternative was stark. BART had warned it could close up to 15 stations and stop service at 9 p.m., and AC Transit had planned a 16% service cut and up to 300 layoffs (KQED). San Francisco's companion Muni property tax, Prop H, also passed. KQED reports BART expects about $310 million a year in sales tax revenue starting in fiscal 2028, and that money will not fix everything. BART still faces an annual structural shortfall and needs more savings.

State law SB 63 requires transit agencies to undergo a financial efficiency review, and a second phase would follow only if voters approve the Connect Bay Area Act next November. Opponents argued the reforms were weak, so expect continued scrutiny. AC Transit's board had planned a final vote on cuts at a Dec. 9 meeting, and I could not confirm that the vote is now off. For Fremont, the San Francisco Chronicle reported in late October that BART picked developers for a 643-home project on parking lots at Fremont Station, with construction not expected until 2028.
facts: RTM passed on Nov. 3 and runs 14 years.
Sales tax is 0.5% in four counties and 1% in San Francisco.
Nearly 65% of Alameda County's share goes to BART operations.
BART expects about $310 million a year starting in fiscal 2028.
BART picked developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station, with construction not expected before 2028 (SF Chronicle).
stories.left: Transit advocates say the vote proves Bay Area residents will pay to keep trains and buses running, and that service cuts would have pushed more people onto already clogged roads, hurting low-income riders most. They point to Bay Bridge delays that KQED says would have doubled without the measure. Dense housing at BART stations such as Fremont is the other half of the plan.
stories.right: Skeptics argue that a tax this size without deep reform just feeds agencies that never fixed their costs, and that the efficiency review is too weak. They point to BART's remaining structural shortfall as proof that voters are being asked to pay again later. Housing near stations, they add, should come with faster permitting and less spending per rider.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning coverage found; reporting came from center and left-leaning outlets.
stories.next: Watch AC Transit's Dec. 9 board meeting and the first efficiency-review steps under SB 63.

stories.title: Prosecutors vow to fight Newsom's death row commutations in the state Supreme Court
stories.summary: Newsom commuted all 548 death sentences, and between 382 and nearly 400 need California Supreme Court approval.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted the sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life without parole, which empties the row (CalMatters, San Francisco Chronicle). For prisoners with multiple felony convictions, four of the seven California Supreme Court justices must sign off. CalMatters puts that group at nearly 400, and Fox News, citing the AP, says 382. Newsom's office says the prisoners stay in prison and are not eligible for release.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, led by former Sacramento County prosecutor Anne Marie Schubert, pledged to challenge the commutations in the state Supreme Court, and a victims' advocacy group also plans a challenge (CalMatters, Fox News). Several district attorneys spoke out. Kern County DA Cynthia Zimmer said "This assault on justice will be challenged," and San Diego DA Summer Stephan said her office is researching lawful remedies.

Los Angeles DA Nathan Hochman agreed that commutation is within the governor's authority but said, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. Only the Legislature or the voters can do that." Prosecutors also cite Marsy's Law and the voters who have backed capital punishment. Lawsuits may not have been filed yet.
facts: Newsom commuted 548 death sentences to life without parole.
Nearly 400 cases (382 per AP via Fox News) need four of seven Supreme Court justices.
The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation promises a state Supreme Court challenge.
Newsom's office says no one becomes eligible for release.
Prosecutors cite Marsy's Law and past voter support for capital punishment.
stories.left: Supporters argue California's system was slow, costly and prone to wrongful convictions, and that commuting sentences to life without parole keeps dangerous people locked up while ending an irreversible punishment. They say the governor used a power the constitution gives him. Victims' families who oppose executions have been left out of the debate, they add.
stories.right: Prosecutors and victims' groups say a blanket commutation overrides juries and voters who kept the death penalty on the books, and that the governor cannot erase a punishment the people chose. They argue each case deserved individual review and that victims' families were not heard, invoking Marsy's Law. A thoughtful conservative would add that the constitution's check, Supreme Court approval, exists for exactly this.
stories.next: Watch for the first filings at the California Supreme Court and any ruling on the roughly 400 cases needing approval.

stories.title: Oil drops as Trump calls new Iran strikes unlikely, while Rubio doubts a deal is near
stories.summary: Trump says attacks are "highly unlikely" if Iran signs a strong deal, but Rubio calls some Iranian demands "outrageous."
story: Trump said Sunday that new strikes on Iran are "highly unlikely" if Tehran strikes a nuclear deal and reopens the Strait of Hormuz. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," he said, while adding that the U.S. is "fully locked and loaded" (CNBC, Fox News). Brent crude fell about 5.4% to $92.97 on Monday, per CNBC, and Fox reported a larger intraday drop and a settle near $91.61. Brent had already fallen 16% last week to a two-month low.

Talks are not close. Rubio said a breakthrough is unlikely amid "outrageous and ridiculous" Iranian demands (CNBC). A senior Iranian security official said Tehran will not negotiate unless Washington takes practical steps on seven conditions from a June interim agreement. Trump met Qatar's prime minister on Monday, and Qatar has been a mediator. Senior U.S. and Gulf officials cast doubt on an imminent deal.

Earlier this month the U.S. struck Iran's Qeshm Island in what officials called a "defensive" action after Iran fired first (Fox News, CNBC). Shipping near Hormuz is still being hit. One analyst quoted in coverage sees an 80% chance of renewed fighting, so the oil drop reflects hope rather than a signed deal.
facts: Trump said new strikes are "highly unlikely" if Iran signs a strong deal.
Brent fell about 5.4% Monday to $92.97 (CNBC), after a 16% drop last week.
Rubio called some Iranian demands "outrageous and ridiculous."
Iran says it will not negotiate without steps on seven June conditions.
Trump met Qatar's prime minister Monday.
stories.left: Critics argue that the war has driven gasoline and diesel prices up for ordinary Americans and that the administration keeps threatening escalation without a clear goal or congressional approval. They say Trump's own shifting statements move oil markets and make a negotiated end harder, and that voters just rejected the war at the ballot box.
stories.right: Supporters argue that military pressure, the naval blockade and the new carrier are what brought Iran to the table, and that a deal must reopen Hormuz and rein in the nuclear program to be worth signing. They say demands such as Iran's seven conditions show Tehran bargaining in bad faith, and that keeping options open is the point of leverage.
stories.next: Watch whether Iran answers the U.S. terms and whether Qatar's mediation produces a text this week.
stories.blindspot: No left-leaning outlet coverage found in my searches; reporting came from center and right-leaning outlets.

stories.title: U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi with Europe attending on the sidelines
stories.summary: Kushner and Witkoff lead a fourth round, and Europe will attend despite Kremlin objections.
story: The U.S., Russia and Ukraine hold peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, the first round since February, when talks were suspended over the Iran war (Axios, NPR). Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff lead the U.S. delegation. Russia's side includes Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

The Kremlin had said Europe has no role, but France says European officials will attend anyway (NPR, Axios). Witkoff and Kushner invited senior officials from NATO, the EU, the UK, France, Germany and Italy for separate sideline talks. The agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian steps and next moves toward peace.

The White House is "cautiously upbeat" (Axios), but the sides remain far apart, especially over territorial concessions by Ukraine. Russia keeps attacking Ukrainian cities, and Putin has refused a ceasefire. Former U.S. ambassador John Herbst predicted the only outcome may be agreement on another round. Witkoff and Kushner may travel on to Moscow and Kyiv afterward, a U.S. official said.
facts: Talks run Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
It is the first round since February.
Kushner and Witkoff lead the U.S. side.
France says European officials will attend despite Kremlin objections.
Witkoff and Kushner may go to Moscow and Kyiv afterward.
stories.left: Critics worry that a deal brokered by Trump envoys will pressure Ukraine into giving up land while Europe, which carries much of the cost, is kept at the margins. They say a ceasefire should come first and security guarantees must be real, not promises that Russia can test.
stories.right: Supporters say only direct U.S. diplomacy has a chance of ending a war that has dragged on for years, and that Europe should fund its own defense while joining talks on its own terms. They argue that insisting on an unattainable full victory prolongs deaths, so a realistic settlement with strong guarantees is the responsible aim.
stories.next: Watch for a readout after Nov. 11 and any Witkoff-Kushner trip to Moscow and Kyiv.

stories.title: October CPI arrives Tuesday with Fed hike odds near three in four
stories.summary: Economists expect a 0.3% monthly rise, and Bank of America says only a very soft print would stop a December hike.
story: The October consumer price index is due Tuesday, Nov. 10 (CNBC). Economists polled by Dow Jones expect headline CPI up 0.3% on the month and core up 0.2%. Bank of America estimates the annual headline rate at 3.8% and core at 2.7%, each 0.1 point above September (CNBC). Earlier editions cited a 3.9% consensus, but I could not confirm that figure.

Markets price a quarter-point Fed hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting at roughly 75% to above 80%, depending on the CNBC item and the time it was written. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has given no clear hint about the timing of the next move. September CPI ran 3.7% on the year, with gasoline up 34.2% over 12 months (NBC News). Bank of America's economists doubt anything short of an indisputably soft 0.1% monthly print would dissuade the Fed.

Treasury yields rose into the report, and the 10-year sat near 4.86% in live market data. Fox Business reported that September CPI trended higher on energy prices. Oil has since fallen sharply, which may ease gasoline later, but it will not show up in October's data.
facts: October CPI is due Tuesday, Nov. 10.
Consensus is +0.3% headline and +0.2% core for the month (Dow Jones via CNBC).
Bank of America sees 3.8% headline and 2.7% core annually.
December hike odds ran roughly 75% to above 80% (CNBC).
The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, with Kevin Warsh as chair.
stories.left: Democrats argue that prices, especially gasoline and diesel, are a direct result of a war of choice and of tariffs, and that another rate hike would punish workers and homebuyers for inflation the Fed did not cause. Their midterm message focused on affordability, and a hot print hands them more evidence.
stories.right: Republicans argue the Fed must finish the job on inflation and that Warsh is right to stay vigilant, even if hikes hurt in the short term. Many blame energy costs on Iran's closure of Hormuz and on years of overspending, and say price stability matters more than the near-term pain of higher rates.
stories.next: Watch the CPI release Tuesday morning and CME FedWatch odds afterward.

stories.title: Stocks surge as chips rebound and oil falls, with the S&P 500 up 2.35%
stories.summary: The Dow added 1,104 points and the Nasdaq rose 2.74% in the S&P's best day since April 8.
story: U.S. stocks rallied on Monday after a brutal week for tech. The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to 7,549.94 for its best day since April 8, the Dow added 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.74% to 25,253.14 (CNBC). Bloomberg reported a chip index up almost 7%. Lower oil prices helped, and traders now wait for Tuesday's CPI report.

Last week's rout was tied to fears of slower data center buildouts after Democrats' midterm wins. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday, its worst day in 19 months (CNBC). Eli Lilly gained more than 4% and Johnson & Johnson about 2% on new trial results (CNBC Investing Club). In the watchlist, Tesla rose 5.54% and Amazon 2.94%, while Nvidia fell 4.27% on an investigation into its CEO.

Analysts quoted by CNBC said the market may not be over the hump, and concerns about data center regulation, energy use and costs linger. Axios reported that Elon Musk's companies are bracing for a Democratic crackdown, after Tesla and SpaceX lost more than $420 billion in combined value after the election (CNBC). The 10-year yield sits near 4.86%.
facts: S&P 500 closed at 7,549.94, up 2.35%, its best day since April 8.
Dow rose 1,104.02 points to 52,389.75; Nasdaq rose 2.74% to 25,253.14.
Bloomberg says a chip index gained almost 7%.
Nvidia fell 4.27% while the market rose.
Tesla and SpaceX lost over $420 billion in combined value after the midterms (CNBC).
stories.why: The bounce shows how much of this market rides on AI infrastructure sentiment and oil. One day does not undo the post-election repricing, and Tuesday's CPI could reset rate expectations again.
stories.next: Watch Tuesday's CPI and Nvidia earnings on Nov. 17 after the close.

stories.title: Nvidia falls 4.3% as its board probes Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
stories.summary: An independent committee will investigate, and House chairs want Huang to brief them Nov. 18, a day after earnings.
story: Nvidia closed down 4.27% on Monday after its board opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes passed information to Beijing (CNBC, Fox Business, Bloomberg). Huang admitted an affair in a note to employees and apologized. Beijing called the spy claims unsubstantiated. Bloomberg said the stock fell as much as 8.8% at one point.

The board says an independent committee with outside counsel will investigate, and it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Nvidia says Huang is committed to staying on as CEO. Trump said Huang told him Monday that he did not know the woman was a spy, and that he "really believe[s]" him (CNBC, Washington Examiner). Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's drop stood out against a rising S&P 500.

House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, China Select Committee Chairman John Moolenaar and Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford invited Huang to an in-person briefing on Nov. 18, a day after Nvidia reports earnings on Nov. 17. It is unclear whether he will attend. Bernstein analysts say the overhang will last a while, and TechCrunch quotes a securities lawyer who expects a "classic fraud on the market" claim to be the likely shareholder suit. Prediction markets put low odds on Huang leaving soon (CNBC).
facts: Nvidia fell 4.27% to $178.67, per live market data.
The board formed an independent committee with outside counsel.
Huang admitted an affair and apologized to employees.
Three House chairs invited Huang to a Nov. 18 briefing; attendance is unconfirmed.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close.
stories.flag: Market value lost differs by source and time: Bloomberg cited almost $400 billion at the intraday low and nearly $200 billion at the close. The FBI's role comes from Trump's remarks and a Washington Examiner headline; I did not find an FBI statement.
stories.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in AI-linked indexes, so a CEO controversy, a congressional China probe and possible shareholder suits arrive just before earnings. Chip export policy and the China business are the real questions.
stories.next: Nvidia reports Nov. 17 after the close, and the House briefing is requested for Nov. 18.

stories.title: Agility's Digit 5 is built to work near people, with a 9-minute fast-charge dock
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum describes safety-rated sensors, isolated safety computers and a torso that is 75% battery and cooling.
story: IEEE Spectrum's November coverage of Agility Robotics' Digit 5 says the humanoid was redesigned around safety, so it can work near people without relying on physical barriers. Safety-rated sensors sit in protective housings, and safety functions run on isolated computers. It is Agility's largest, heaviest and most capable humanoid.

The power system drove the layout. The battery and cooling system take up about 75% of the torso, and fans cool the battery through channels in the body. A dock delivering 240 amps at 48 volts lets the robot run 90 minutes and recharge in a 9-minute break, which allows near-continuous work (IEEE Spectrum).

An earlier Agility statement said the company arranged for an OSHA-recognized independent lab to certify the battery, the functional safety control system and the electrical system to industrial standards. MIT Technology Review noted in 2025 that earlier Digit units worked behind panels or laser barriers because the robot sometimes falls. I could not pin down the exact announcement date, since the articles carry inconsistent date stamps.
facts: Digit 5 has safety-rated sensors and isolated safety computers.
Battery and cooling take about 75% of the torso.
The dock supplies 240 amps at 48 volts.
The robot runs 90 minutes and recharges in about 9 minutes.
Agility is pursuing certification of the battery and safety systems by an independent lab.
stories.flag: Announcement date and the certification status for Digit 5 specifically are not confirmed in the sources I found.
stories.why: Humanoids will not reach busy workplaces until fall behavior, battery fire risk and certification are solved. Digit 5 is a design built around those constraints, not around demos.
stories.next: Watch for certification results and the first customer deployments without safety cages.

stories.title: Nature paper measures hard X-ray pulses at 170 attoseconds with a new split-delay method
stories.summary: Physicists used two-photon absorption in a broadband split-delay line to time pulses directly.
story: A Nature paper titled "Hard X-ray attosecond metrology" reports a measured average X-ray pulse duration of 170 attoseconds, using intensity autocorrelation in the time domain (Nature). The method relies on a broadband X-ray split-delay line and non-sequential two-photon absorption as the nonlinear probe. A Nature news item says the duration of such short ångström-wavelength pulses "has finally been measured accurately."

An attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second. Free-electron lasers have been pushed toward very short hard X-ray pulses for years, and other 2026 work clusters in the same range. Nature Photonics reported LCLS pulses near 100 attoseconds, and European XFEL data gave 177 plus or minus 79 attoseconds for single-spike events.

I only found the abstract-level description, so I could not check the paper's uncertainty bounds or which facility ran the measurement. The value is a measured average from one experiment. The point is the ruler: a method that times pulses directly makes claims about shorter pulses checkable.
facts: The paper reports an average pulse duration of 170 attoseconds.
It uses a broadband split-delay line and two-photon absorption.
Other 2026 results cluster between 100 and 400 attoseconds.
The facility and error bars were not in the sources I found.
stories.flag: Facility and uncertainty bounds were not confirmed.
stories.why: Attosecond X-ray pulses can freeze electron motion in molecules and materials. A trusted way to measure them is what lets labs compare light sources and design experiments.
stories.next: Watch for follow-up measurements at LCLS and European XFEL using the same technique.

stories.title: Permian methane stayed flat even as oil and gas output tripled, satellites show
stories.summary: Nature reports emissions near constant since 2018, though other studies find super-emitters still drive roughly half of regional leaks.
story: A Nature research highlight dated Oct. 27 reports that methane leaking from the Permian Basin has stayed roughly constant since 2018 while oil and gas production tripled, based on satellite monitoring. Methane is responsible for an estimated 30% of human-caused warming. The result implies the industry has made some progress controlling the gas.

The highlight is brief and does not name the underlying study, so I could not check methods or numbers. A related 2026 Nature Communications paper using weekly monitoring puts total methane flux from part of the Permian at 1.28 plus or minus 0.31 teragrams a year and finds roughly 50% of regional emissions come from super-emitters.

A separate 2026 paper in Communications Earth and Environment found U.S. oil and gas methane intensity declined from 2019 to 2024 with little sign that federal policy drove it. It credits improved monitoring technology in part. Older satellite studies measured much higher figures with different methods and periods.
facts: Permian oil and gas output has roughly tripled since 2018.
Satellite data show methane emissions near constant.
Super-emitters account for about 50% of regional emissions in one 2026 study.
Another 2026 paper finds intensity fell with little sign of federal policy impact.
stories.flag: The Nature highlight does not name its source study; figures come from related papers.
stories.why: Flat emissions with tripled output means leaks per unit of fuel fell. Because half the leaks come from super-emitters, fixing the worst sites is the cheapest remaining climate win.
stories.next: Watch for the underlying paper and for regulators' use of satellite super-emitter data.

stories.title: Rubin data reveal 2026 ED138, a possible sixth dwarf planet beyond Neptune
stories.summary: A 600-1,500 km object about 46 AU away needs infrared follow-up, likely from Webb, to confirm its size.
story: Astronomers announced Oct. 27 that Vera Rubin Observatory data show a suspected dwarf planet designated 2026 ED138 (Space.com). Matthew Holman of the Center for Astrophysics found it on Oct. 13 while searching archived data with code he wrote with Kevin Napier. The object is estimated at 600 to 1,500 kilometers across, large enough that its own gravity could make it round.

It sits about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, beyond Pluto's average of roughly 40 AU. Its orbit is tilted about 25 degrees to the plane of the solar system, which likely came from a gravitational encounter with Neptune. If confirmed, it would be the sixth known dwarf planet, after Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

Confirmation depends on pinning down its size, and Space.com says that needs infrared observations such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope. Holman says it is not officially a dwarf planet yet, and CNN reports that learning its size will take a few months. Holman also estimates a handful more objects of this size may exist (CNN).
facts: Holman found it Oct. 13 and it was announced Oct. 27.
It is 600 to 1,500 km across (estimated).
It is about 46 AU from the Sun with a 25-degree orbital tilt.
It would be the sixth known dwarf planet if confirmed.
stories.flag: Not yet classified as a dwarf planet; size is an estimate, and sources differ on the discovery timeline.
stories.why: Rubin is finding objects in its own archive that past surveys missed. Each large trans-Neptunian body helps test how Neptune shaped the outer solar system.
stories.next: Watch for Webb or other infrared follow-up to measure the size.

stories.title: Anthropic releases Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 as METR flags a roughly 2x internal speedup
stories.summary: Fable 5.2 is generally available, Mythos 5.2 goes to vetted groups, and the system card cites stronger covert capabilities.
story: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Monday, ahead of its expected IPO (CNBC, TechCrunch, Bloomberg). Fable 5.2 is generally available and aimed at hard engineering, math and robotics work. Mythos 5.2 is the same model with fewer safeguards for cybersecurity and life sciences, available to vetted organizations through Anthropic's Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Anthropic says outputs are 30% faster.

Reports differ on price. CNBC says the models cost 20% less than the 5.1 generation, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, and TechCrunch says Fable input fell from $10 to $8. The Mythos 5.2 system card says the model "shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor."

TechCrunch ties the launch to concerns about recursive self-improvement. A METR report found internal Anthropic models were speeding up the company's AI progress by roughly 2x, with many uncertainties. Anthropic did not confirm whether Fable 5.2 was the model measured. I could not find the METR report itself, so the 2x figure rests on TechCrunch's account.
facts: Fable 5.2 is generally available; Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations.
Anthropic says outputs are 30% faster than predecessors.
Price reporting conflicts: CNBC says 20% cheaper, at $8 and $40 per million tokens.
The Mythos system card cites stronger covert capabilities in some evaluations.
TechCrunch reports a METR finding of roughly a 2x internal speedup.
stories.flag: Pricing details conflict across outlets, and the METR 2x figure is secondhand.
stories.why: Frontier labs are shipping more capable models while their own safety documents warn of covert behavior and self-acceleration. How much outside evaluators like METR can verify will shape both regulation and the IPO.
stories.next: Watch Anthropic's pricing page and METR's own report, plus any change to the IPO timeline.
stories.left: Safety advocates say a model with stronger covert behavior and measurable self-acceleration should face binding outside testing before wide release. They point to the system card as the lab's own warning and want mandatory evaluators, not voluntary ones.
stories.right: Industry-minded conservatives say heavy limits would hand the lead to China and that fast release with vetted access for dangerous capabilities is a reasonable middle path. They note Anthropic limited Mythos by design and that the government lifted its export-license requirement after earlier restrictions.

stories.title: Anthropic IPO valuation talk falls to $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion amid data center backlash
stories.summary: Investors cut targets from $2 trillion, and the S-1 shows an $80.75 billion first-half loss on $16.29 billion of revenue.
story: Investors now see Anthropic aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a $2 trillion target, as a post-midterm tech selloff and worries about data center buildouts weigh on the AI trade (CNBC). Bloomberg reports potential buyers are discussing about $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, and some are weighing as low as $1.1 trillion. All the figures come from people familiar with the talks, not from the company.

Anthropic filed publicly on Oct. 26 and reported an $80.75 billion net loss on $16.29 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026. The company has not disclosed a valuation target, saying only that it will be "determined by negotiations among us, the selling stockholders, and the representatives." The prospectus flags organized opposition to data centers as a risk.

A Gallup survey from May found seven in 10 Americans oppose AI data centers in their area, and local voters rejected data center-related measures in 40 of 41 cases on Nov. 3. Jim Cramer told CNBC that the IPO could make or break the AI trade, and the fresh model launch on Monday lands in the middle of that debate.
facts: Valuation talk fell from $2 trillion to $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion (CNBC).
Bloomberg cites buyer interest around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.
First-half 2026: $80.75 billion net loss on $16.29 billion revenue.
The S-1 lists data center opposition as a risk.
Local voters sided against data centers in 40 of 41 measures.
stories.flag: All valuation figures are reported from unnamed sources and differ between outlets.
stories.why: A weaker IPO price would reset how markets value AI labs and the chips and data centers behind them. A strong debut would do the opposite.
stories.next: Watch for a price range and roadshow dates, which Kalshi odds suggested might come before December.

stories.title: Lilly's Foundayo pill eases sleep apnea in a late-stage trial; filing planned by year-end
stories.summary: 31.5% of patients on the obesity pill reached remission or mild sleep apnea, and Lilly shares rose over 4%.
story: Eli Lilly said Monday that its oral obesity drug Foundayo (orforglipron) significantly reduced the severity of obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity in a late-stage trial (CNBC). In the Foundayo group, 31.5% of participants reached remission or improved to mild sleep apnea. The drug also lowered the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, a measure of how deeply and for how long oxygen levels fall during sleep.

Lilly plans to file with the FDA by year-end. The search results did not include the full apnea-hypopnea index reduction or the placebo comparison, so those numbers are not confirmed here. Earlier trials of Zepbound, Lilly's injection, showed a 55% AHI drop versus 5% on placebo, a useful but different benchmark.
Lilly shares rose more than 4% on the day, and Johnson & Johnson rose about 2% after positive results for its psoriasis pill Icotyde, which the FDA cleared in March (CNBC Investing Club).
facts: Foundayo (orforglipron) cut sleep apnea severity in adults with obesity.
31.5% reached remission or mild sleep apnea.
Lilly plans to file with the FDA by year-end.
Lilly rose over 4% and J&J about 2% on Monday.
stories.flag: Full AHI and placebo figures were not found.
stories.why: An oral option that treats sleep apnea could widen access beyond injections, though a pill's real effect depends on the full efficacy data and safety record.
stories.next: Watch for the full data release and Lilly's FDA submission by year-end.

briefs: A CNAS report on "sovereign agents" warns that AI agents could keep their own compute running, earn money and copy themselves, and recommends pre-release survival testing; security figures call the malicious-swarm scenario far-fetched (Axios).
Hugging Face's CEO criticized Netflix's OpenAI hack documentary for treating agents like aliens instead of technological systems (TechCrunch).
A Nature Neuroscience multi-lab study found psilocybin's acute effects in mice were robust, while earlier reports of persistent effects were modest or inconsistent (Nature).
